prompt.context: Our client is A+ Airline Co., the third largest airline in the United States by passengers carried. This week, we have been flying on our primary competitor, Gamma Airline, and we noticed something interesting: they stopped accepting cash for in-flight food and beverage services and now only accept major credit cards.
prompt.question: The CEO of A+ Airline Co. wants to know: why did Gamma Airline switch from a Cash & Card system to a Credit Card only system, and should we follow them?

clarifying_info.q: What payment methods does A+ Airline currently accept?
clarifying_info.a: Both cash and major credit cards for in-flight food and beverage purchases.

clarifying_info.q: Do customers need a credit card to buy a ticket?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — roughly 99% of all consumers purchase their airline tickets using a credit card, so all passengers on the plane have a credit card available to them.

clarifying_info.q: What items are sold on board?
clarifying_info.a: Only food and alcoholic beverage items are sold on A+ Airline flights.

clarifying_info.q: Is this a domestic or international decision?
clarifying_info.a: US Domestic only. Ignore international flights.

clarifying_info.q: Has any other airline made this switch?
clarifying_info.a: Gamma is the only airline that has made the switch so far; however, all other airlines are evaluating it. For this case, Gamma and A+ Airline should be considered exactly the same in all regards.

clarifying_info.q: Do First Class passengers pay for food and beverage?
clarifying_info.a: No. First Class passengers receive free food and beverage.

exhibits.title: An Average A+ Airline Flight
exhibits.shows: Seat configuration and passenger data for a typical A+ Airline Boeing 737-800. Includes total seats, load factors by class, business/leisure splits, purchase rates, average spend, and the current cash/card split of in-flight purchases.

data.note: First Class passengers receive free food and beverage

exhibits.title: A+ Airline Cash & Card Operations
exhibits.shows: Side-by-side process diagrams for the current Cash Management process (8 steps, 31 days total time) and the Credit Card process (3 steps, 24 hours total time), including fee structures and staffing requirements for cash handling.

framework: Revenue Changes: Loss of cash-only customers (some will not convert to card) vs. potential increase in card customers due to faster transactions
Cost Changes: Cash management overhead costs eliminated vs. incremental credit card processing fees (note both carry a 2% fee, so net fee impact is a wash)
Cash Flow & Working Capital Changes: Faster payment collection (31 days → 24 hours) improves time value of money and reduces working capital tied up in change and cash on planes

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total market size in dollars for food and beverage purchases on an average flight, and the current split between cash and card spend.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate occupants by class, apply purchase rates, then split by payment method. Key steps: (1) First Class: 50 seats × 100% load = 50 occupants, all business, receive free F&B — $0 revenue. (2) Economy: 150 seats × 80% load = 120 occupants; 50% business = 60, 50% leisure = 60. (3) Business buyers: 60 × 41% ≈ 45 × $10 = $450. Leisure buyers: 60 × 25% = 15 × $5 = $75. Total = $525. (4) Cash spend: 20% × $525 = $105; Card spend: 80% × $525 = $420.

math.setup: Total economy occupants = 150 × 80% = 120. Business = 60, Leisure = 60. Purchasing business = 60 × 41% ≈ 45 @ $10 = $450. Purchasing leisure = 60 × 25% = 15 @ $5 = $75. Total spend = $525. Cash = 20% × $525 = $105. Card = 80% × $525 = $420.
math.answer: Total in-flight spend = $525/flight. Cash spend = $105/flight, Card spend = $420/flight.

questions.prompt: The casebook notes we will lose 1/3 of current cash customers. How many customers and how much revenue is lost per flight?
questions.guidance: Cash customers = 20% of total purchasers. Total purchasers = 60 (45 business + 15 leisure). Cash purchasers ≈ 20% of 60 = 12. Lost = 1/3 of 12 = 4 customers. Revenue loss: business cash buyers = 3 × $10 = $30; leisure cash buyers = 1 × $5 = $5. Total revenue loss = $35/flight.

math.setup: Total purchasers = 60. Cash purchasers = 20% × 60 = 12. Lost = 1/3 × 12 = 4. Business lost: 3 × $10 = $30. Leisure lost: 1 × $5 = $5.
steps: Cash purchasers (20%): 60 × 20% = 12 (approx. 9 business, 3 leisure — allocated proportionally)
Lose 1/3 of cash customers: 1/3 × 12 = 4 customers lost (3 business, 1 leisure)
math.answer: Revenue loss = $35/flight (3 business customers at $10 each + 1 leisure customer at $5).

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what cost changes result from switching to card-only? What is the net cost impact per flight?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: (1) Both cash and card carry a 2% fee — this is a wash, no net savings. (2) Cash management requires 7 additional employees per airport (5 cash handlers + 2 processing center staff) that can be eliminated. The interviewer should tell the candidate that total overhead savings from eliminating cash management = $35/flight. Candidate should note that $35 cost savings goes straight to the bottom line (profit), whereas the $35 revenue loss is a top-line reduction — meaning the net operating income impact is actually better than it appears at first glance.

math.setup: 2% fee exists on both cash and card — net fee delta = $0. Overhead savings from eliminating 7 employees across airport cash operations = $35/flight (given by interviewer when asked).
steps: Credit card fee: 2% on card revenue — already being paid on card portion
Cash management fee: 2% on cash revenue — equivalent rate, so switching eliminates cash fee but adds card fee on converted cash customers: net = $0
Eliminating cash management overhead (5 cash handlers + 2 processing staff per airport): savings = $35/flight
math.answer: Net cost savings = $35/flight from eliminated overhead. The 2% fee is a wash.

questions.prompt: Qualitatively, what is the impact of collecting payment 30 days sooner (card: 24 hours vs. cash: 31 days)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify Time Value of Money and Working Capital benefits: (1) Money received sooner can be invested in interest-earning accounts or growth projects. (2) Can pay suppliers early and capture early-payment discounts. (3) Can pay down lines of credit faster. (4) Eliminating $50/flight in change eliminates tied-up working capital. (5) Reduction in cash theft and damage losses. (6) Faster transactions on the plane may also increase customer satisfaction and purchase rates.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional costs might A+ Airline face when switching to credit card only?

categories.name: Technology & Infrastructure
ideas: Wifi connectivity cost to verify card transactions with banks in real time
Upgrades to wireless payment terminals on aircraft
System integration with merchant services provider

categories.name: Fraud & Security
ideas: Increased fraud risk with card-only system
Need for PCI DSS compliance measures

categories.name: Customer Experience
ideas: Potential customer complaints from cash-preference passengers
Need for staff training on new process
Communication/marketing costs to inform passengers of policy change

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Transition period costs (running dual systems temporarily)
Potential downtime if card terminal fails mid-flight
Contractual renegotiation with armored car service

recommendation: A+ Airline should switch to a credit card only system for in-flight food and beverage purchases.

Quantitatively, the revenue loss of $35/flight (from 4 lost cash customers) is exactly offset by $35/flight in cost savings from eliminating cash management overhead — but critically the savings go straight to the bottom line while the revenue loss is a top-line reduction, making the switch net positive on operating income.

Qualitatively, the switch improves cash flow by collecting payment 30 days sooner, frees up $50/flight in working capital currently tied up as change, reduces cash theft and damage risk, and is likely to increase purchase rates and average transaction size due to faster service.
risks: A small segment of cash-preference customers (roughly 1/3 of the 20% who currently pay cash) will be alienated and lose purchases.
If wireless card terminals fail mid-flight, no revenue can be collected at all.
Fraud and chargeback risk increases with card-only acceptance.
Negative press or customer backlash from passengers who feel forced to use cards.
next_steps: Pilot the card-only policy on a subset of routes to validate assumptions about customer loss and satisfaction.
Negotiate favorable merchant service rates to ensure the 2% fee does not increase.
Invest in reliable backup terminal solutions and staff training.
Monitor competitor adoption — since all other airlines are evaluating the switch, moving first creates a process advantage.
Explore whether card-only policy can extend to international routes after domestic validation.
